parts.subtitle: With the right encouragement, your mind can convince the body to heal itself. What is the mysterious force that can do this?
parts.article:
The Placebo Effect
 
With the right encouragement, your mind can convince the body to heal itself. What is the mysterious force that can do this?
 
A Want to devise a new form of alternative medical treatment? No problem. Here's the recipe. As a practitioner, be warm, sympathetic, reassuring and enthusiastic. Your treatment should involve physical contact, and each session with your patients should take at least half an hour. Encourage your patients to take an active part in their treatment and understand how their disorders relate to the rest of their lives. Tell them that their own bodies possess the true power to heal. Get them to pay you well. Describe your treatment in familiar words, but embroidered with a hint of mysticism: energy fields, energy flows, energy blocks, meridians, forces, auras, rhythms and the like. Refer to the knowledge of an earlier age: wisdom carelessly swept aside by the rise of blind mechanistic science. Oh, come off it, you're saying. Something like that couldn't possibly work, could it? Well, yes, it could and often well enough to earn you a living. And a very good living if you are sufficiently convincing or, better still, really believe in your therapy. Many illnesses get better on their own, so if you are lucky and administer your treatment at just the right time you'll get the credit. But that's only part of it. Some of the improvement really would be down to you. Not necessarily because you'd recommended ginseng rather than chamomile tea or used this crystal as opposed to that pressure point. Nothing so specific. Your healing power would be the outcome of a paradoxical force that conventional medicine recognizes but remains oddly ambivalent about: the placebo effect. Placebos are treatments that have no direct effect on the body, yet still work because the patient has faith in their power to heal. Most often the term refers to a dummy pill, but it applies just as much to any device or procedure, from a sticking plaster to a crystal. The existence of the placebo effect implies that even a complete fraud could make a difference to someone's health, which is why some practitioners of alternative medicine are sensitive about any mention of the subject. In fact, the placebo is a powerful part of all medical care, orthodox or otherwise, though its role is often neglected and misunderstood.
 
B At one level, it should come as no surprise that our state of mind can influence our physiology: anger opens the superficial blood vessels of the face; sadness pumps the tear glands. But exactly how placebos work their medical magic is still largely unknown. Most of the scant research to date has focused on the control of pain, because it's one of the commonest complaints and lends itself to experimental study. Here, attention has turned to the endorphins, natural substances produced in the brain that are known to help control pain. Any of the neurochemicals involved in transmitting pain impulses or modulating them might also be involved in generating the placebo response, says Don Price, an oral surgeon at the University of Florida. That case has been strengthened by the recent work of Fabrizio Benedetti of the University of Turin, who showed that the placebo effect can be abolished by a drug, naloxone, which blocks the effects of endorphins. Benedetti induced pain in a pressure cuff on the forearm. He did this several times a day for several days, using morphine each time to control the pain. On the final day, without saying anything, he replaced the morphine with a saline solution. This still relieved the subjects' pain: a placebo effect. But when he added naloxone to the saline, and blocked the endorphins, the pain relief disappeared. Here was direct proof that the relief of pain by a placebo is carried out, at least in part, by these natural opiates.
 
C Though scientists don't know exactly how placebos work, they have accumulated a fair bit of knowledge about how to trigger the effect. A London rheumatologist found, for example, that red dummy capsules made more effective painkillers than blue, green or yellow ones. Research on American students revealed that blue pills make better tranquillisers than pink, a colour more suitable for stimulants. Even branding can make a difference: if Aspro or Tylenol are what you like to take for a headache; their chemically identical generic equivalents may be less effective.
 
D It matters too how the treatment is delivered. Decades ago, when the major tranquilliser chlorpromazine was being introduced, a doctor in Kansas categorised his colleagues according to whether they were keen on it, openly sceptical of its benefits, or took a let's-try-and-see attitude. His conclusion: the more enthusiastic the doctor, the better the drug performed. A recent survey by Ernst on doctors' bedside manners turned up one consistent finding: physicians who adopt a warm, friendly, reassuring manner are more effective than those whose consultations are formal and do not offer reassurance. Warm, friendly and reassuring are precisely what alternative treatment is all about, of course. Many of the ingredients of that opening recipe — the physical contact, the generous swaths of time, the strong hints of supernormal healing power — are just the kind of thing likely to impress patients. It's hardly surprising then, that complementary practitioners are generally best at mobilising the placebo effect, says Arthur Kleinman, professor of social anthropology at Harvard University.

questions.question: An appointment with an alternative practitioner

analyses.content: 原文说每次给病人的治疗必须至少半小时，直接对应选项D的“最少时长（minimum length of time）”。
你可能会因为原文提到了“physical contact（身体接触）”去寻找相关选项，但选项里没有，所以直接抓核心的时间限制即可。
Your treatment should involve physical contact, and each session with your patients should take at least half an hour.

questions.question: An alternative practitioner's explanation of their treatment

analyses.content: 原文说要用“熟悉的词汇（familiar words）”来描述治疗，就是为了让人听得懂，对应选项A的“容易理解（easy to understand）”。
你可能看到原句后面跟着“mysticism（神秘主义）”等复杂的词，就觉得这种疗法很难懂，但这只是为了加点神秘感，核心依然是基础熟悉的词汇。
Describe your treatment in familiar words, but embroidered with a hint of mysticism: energy fields, energy flows, energy blocks, meridians, forces, auras, rhythms and the like.

questions.question: If alternative practitioners have faith in their treatment, they

analyses.content: 原文说如果你“真的相信你的疗法（really believe in your therapy）”，你就能赚到“非常丰厚的生计（very good living）”，对应选项H的“获得高收入（get a high income）”。
你可能会看漏第一句的“earn a living（谋生）”，这段话明确把“医生的信念”和“赚钱”直接绑定在了一起。
Well, yes, it could and often well enough to earn you a living. And a very good living if you are sufficiently convincing or, better still, really believe in your therapy.
原文说很多病自己就会好（get better on their own），直接对应选项B的“没有治疗也能改善（can improve without treatment）”。
你可能会多想去寻找安慰剂的具体作用，但这句只是陈述一个最基本的客观事实，即很多病本身就有自愈的能力。
Many illnesses get better on their own, so if you are lucky and administer your treatment at just the right time you’ll get the credit.

questions.question: Conventional doctors are aware of the placebo effect and they

analyses.content: 原文说传统医学认识到安慰剂的作用，但却对其感到矛盾、忽视和误解，言下之意就是“应该给它更多的认可（give it greater recognition）”。
你可能会觉得原文没有直接出现“should（应该）”这个词，但这道题考查的是“既然重要却被忽视了，那就需要被重视”的逻辑推导。

Your healing power would be the outcome of a paradoxical force that conventional medicine recognizes but remains oddly ambivalent about: the placebo effect. ... In fact, the placebo is a powerful part of all medical care, orthodox or otherwise, though its role is often neglected and misunderstood.

analyses.content: 原文说研究重点在疼痛控制，因为它是最常见的“抱怨/诉求（complaints，在医学上指症状）”，这完美对应D选项的“病人经常经历疼痛并喜欢抱怨”。
你可能会因为看到后文的“内啡肽”就去选B或C，但题目问的是“为什么（because）”吸引关注，原因在第一句话就直接交代了。
Most of the scant research to date has focused on the control of pain, because it’s one of the commonest complaints and lends itself to experimental study.

questions.question: Scientists now have enough information to understand how the placebo effect becomes active in people.

analyses.content: 原文明确指出安慰剂具体是如何发挥医疗作用的，至今仍然“很大程度上是未知的（largely unknown）”，这与题目说的“有足够信息去理解”完全相反。
你可能会因为后面写了科学家关于内啡肽的研究就以为他们已经完全懂了，但其实核心原理至今仍未被完全破解。

At one level, it should come as no surprise that our state of mind can influence our physiology: anger opens the superficial blood vessels of the face; sadness pumps the tear glands. But exactly how placebos work their medical magic is still largely unknown.

questions.question: As a result of experiments, some painkillers have been taken off the market.

analyses.content: 原文只讨论了不同颜色和品牌的药片在安慰剂效应上的有效性区别，全文没有任何一处提到过“有止痛药被退市下架（taken off the market）”。
你可能会看到原文拿不同品牌的药效做比较，就自己脑补出“效果不好的药肯定被下架了”，做阅读判断时切忌强加主观常识。

A London rheumatologist found, for example, that red dummy capsules made more effective painkillers than blue, green or yellow ones. Research on American students revealed that blue pills make better tranquillisers than pink, a colour more suitable for stimulants. Even branding can make a difference: if Aspro or Tylenol are what you like to take for a headache; their chemically identical generic equivalents may be less effective.

questions.question: Individual preference can have an impact on the effectiveness of different brands of headache tablets.

analyses.content: 原文说如果你吃头痛药时“喜欢（like to take）”某个大牌子，那换成成分完全一样的没牌子的药，效果就会变差，这就是个人的偏好影响了药效。
你可能不认识“generic equivalents（无品牌/仿制的等效药）”，但只要看懂“what you like（你喜欢的）”就对应题目里的“个人偏好（Individual preference）”即可。
Even branding can make a difference: if Aspro or Tylenol are what you like to take for a headache; their chemically identical generic equivalents may be less effective.

questions.question: Doctors expressed a range of views on the drug chlorpromazine when it was first introduced.

analyses.content: 原文具体列举了医生们对chlorpromazine这种药的三种态度：热衷、公开怀疑、先试试看，这就直接证实了题目中的“一系列不同的观点（a range of views）”。
你可能会单纯在原文里找“views”这个词，但原文是用具体的分类举例（keen, sceptical, let's-try）来实质性地体现看法的多样性。

Decades ago, when the major tranquilliser chlorpromazine was being introduced, a doctor in Kansas categorised his colleagues according to whether they were keen on it, openly sceptical of its benefits, or took a let's-try-and-see attitude.

questions.question: Ernst's study had a big influence on doctors' behaviour with patients.

analyses.content: 原文只说了Ernst的调查得出一个结论“态度温暖的医生治疗更有效”，但完全没提这个调查有没有“大大改变医生的行为（had a big influence on doctors' behaviour）”。
你可能会顺理成章地觉得：既然发现了态度好能治病，医生看完报告肯定就照着改了；但文章没写的事情绝对不能当做YES。

A recent survey by Ernst on doctors’ bedside manners turned up one consistent finding: physicians who adopt a warm, friendly, reassuring manner are more effective than those whose consultations are formal and do not offer reassurance.

questions.question: Alternative practitioners work in a way that is likely to trigger the placebo effect.

analyses.content: 文章最后一段明确总结，替代医学的从业者总体上“最擅长调动安慰剂效应（best at mobilising the placebo effect）”，完全符合题目说的“ likely to trigger（可能触发）”。
你可能会不认识原文里的“complementary practitioners”，在这里它和题目里的“Alternative practitioners（替代医学从业者）”就是标准的同义替换。

Warm, friendly and reassuring are precisely what alternative treatment is all about, of course. Many of the ingredients of that opening recipe — the physical contact, the generous swaths of time, the strong hints of supernormal healing power — are just the kind of thing likely to impress patients. It’s hardly surprising then, that complementary practitioners are generally best at mobilising the placebo effect, says Arthur Kleinman, professor of social anthropology at Harvard University.
